newsitem.title: USA: American pilots ratify new contract.
newsitem.headline: American pilots ratify new contract.

text.p: The pilots of American Airlines said Monday they approved a five-year labor contract, putting to rest months of contentious negotiations marked by a brief strike, intervention by President Clinton and millions of dollars in lost revenues at the nation's second largest airline.
The ratification of the contract by the Allied Pilots Association's (APA) members removes the threat of a second strike at American Airlines.
American Airlines said 69.3 percent of the union members approved the contract.
The pilots and American Airlines had been in talks to finalize a contract since the current contract became amendable August 31, 1994.

The new five-year contract includes a nine percent wage increase and 5.75 million stock options valued at $10 below market price. The deal also includes a compromise on the most hotly-contested issue regarding which pilots will fly new jets American plans to buy for its regional jet carrier, American Eagle.

American had wanted American Eagle pilots, who are paid less than APA members, to fly the smaller, regional jets so the company can remain competitive with low-cost carriers. The APA pilots were concerned the American Eagle pilots would eventually take over their current routes.
The new contract guarantees that furlouged APA pilots will be able to fly the new jets that the carrier is buying for American Eagle.
In April, the union's 18-member board voted 12 to six to approve the tentative proposal, which was passed on the union members for ratification.

Although most industry analysts and labor experts had expected the rank-and-file pilots to approve the contract, some investors were cautious since the pilots have rejected board-approved deals in the past.
In January, the APA members rejected a tentative contract even though the union board had recommended approval.
The pilots went on strike on February 15, but were forced back to work within minutes by a Presidential Emergency Board established by President Clinton to resolve the dispute.

Although the strike was brief, American Airlines lost money as passengers turned away from the airline in the weeks leading up to the strike. In the first quarter, American said the labor dispute hurt earnings by $70 million.
American said Monday it also may take a "small, additional hit" in the second quarter.

American also was forced to delay delivery on at least 14 Boeing Co scheduled for next year. Under a deal signed last November, American agreed to buy 103 aircraft worth over $6 billion by the year 2001 and acquired options on 527 more.

That aircraft order was contingent on pilots accepting a new contract. When the pilots rejected the initial tentative wage contract in January, American help off on the firm jet purchase orders, so Boeing sold many of the delivery positions it had slated for American.
American said it will make a decision "in the next week or so" regarding the Boeing jet order.
